item.title: Novartis: setback in the neuromuscular sector
item.description: Novartis fails the Harbor study for the drug del-désiran in myotonic dystrophy type 1. It is the second negative trial in a few days, but the company maintains a 5-6% annual growth target for 2025-2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Novartis fails Harbor trial for del-désiran drug on type 1 myotonic dystrophy - Does not achieve primary objective despite "signs of clinical efficacy" - It is the second clinical failure in a few days for the Basel giant - Growth target of 5-6% per year 2025-2030 remains confirmed
## Key facts - **What**: Failure of the Harbor clinical trial - Drug tested: delpacibart etédésiran (del-désiran) - Therapeutic indication: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) - Outcome: Primary objective not achieved - Sequence: Second trial failure in a few days - Corporate headquarters: Basel, Switzerland - Economic prospects: Annual growth 5-6% confirmed 2025-2030
The multinational pharmaceutical company Novartis, based in Basel, has announced the failure of the clinical trial called "Harbor", dedicated to the drug delpacibart etédésiran (del-désiran) for the treatment of myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1). According to the company's official statement, the study did not meet its primary objective, although it demonstrated detectable "signals of clinical efficacy" during development.
This setback represents the second major late-stage clinical trial failure announced by Novartis in a matter of days. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is a degenerative genetic disease of the neuromuscular system, and the tested drug represented a possible therapeutic path for patients suffering from this rare disease.
### The meaning of clinical failure
Not reaching the primary objective of a clinical trial is a disappointing outcome from a scientific and strategic perspective, but it is an intrinsic part of the pharmaceutical development process. Novartis has invested years and significant resources researching del-désiran for the neuromuscular indication, and this announcement marks a major milestone in the development program.
However, it is crucial to understand that “signals of clinical efficacy” observed during the study are not sufficient to proceed towards regulatory approval. International regulatory bodies, including the Swiss agency Swissmedic, require that the drug clearly achieves the primary endpoints before the formal review phase.
### Confidence confirmed despite obstacles
Despite recent clinical failures in the neuromuscular sector, Novartis has maintained full confidence in its overall economic prospects. The company confirmed its annual growth target of between 5% and 6% for the period 2025-2030. This signal is relevant for Swiss stakeholders: the multinational recognizes the obstacles in research, but considers its commercial strategy solid.
Confirmation of the growth target remains an indicator of Novartis' portfolio diversification. With dozens of therapeutic programs in development in different areas, failure to achieve the objective of the Harbor study does not compromise the company's expected consolidated performance in the coming years. ### Implications for the Swiss research economy
Novartis represents one of the pillars of the Swiss pharmaceutical industry and the overall national economy. Headquartered in Basel, it employs tens of thousands of people in Switzerland and maintains a comprehensive network of research, development and manufacturing facilities. Clinical trial failures, although they do not cause immediate dramatic economic effects, influence the company's market valuation, institutional investor confidence and sentiment in the Swiss life sciences sector.
Novartis' neuromuscular research strategy was a recognized priority. The drug del-désiran had been identified as a promising drug candidate for a rare and severe disease. Failure to achieve the primary endpoint in the Harbor study means that the regulatory path to approval for this therapeutic indication has been interrupted, at least temporarily, requiring a strategic reevaluation of the program.
However, it is important to highlight that Novartis operates on a very large and diverse portfolio of research projects. A single clinical failure, while significant from a scientific and commercial perspective, does not compromise the overall strength of the company's business model or Novartis' position in the global pharmaceutical market.
### Switzerland's role as a clinical research hub
Switzerland is a recognized international hub for the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industry. item.title: Updated UN sanctions: SESAM amended on 7 September
item.description: The UN committee amended the sanctions lists on 7 September 2026. The SESAM database automatically updates the restrictive measures in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Update of UN sanctions lists on 7 September 2026 - SESAM database automatically updated in Switzerland - Immediate validity by federal ordinance of 4 March 2016 - Banks and businesses must verify compliance
## Key facts - **What**: Changes to the UN sanctions list (persons, companies, organizations) - When: 7 September 2026 - Where: Bern (Swiss federal coordination) - Who: UN Sanctions Committee and Federal Council - Validity: Immediate in Switzerland via ordinance
Bern, 7 September 2026. The United Nations Sanctions Committee has modified the list of individuals, companies and organizations subject to sanctions. The SESAM database, the Swiss central international compliance system, has been updated accordingly. According to the official communication from the Federal Administration, the changes acquire immediate legal validity in Swiss territory.
The underlying mechanism dates back to 4 March 2016, when the Federal Council approved a decisive ordinance: the automatic transposition of the United Nations Security Council sanctions lists. This rule eliminates bureaucratic delays between the UN decision and implementation in Switzerland. No new federal decrees, parliamentary ratifications or further administrative steps are needed. The change to the UN list comes into force instantly, binding economic operators and financial institutions to comply.
### How SESAM transfigures sanctions into legal obligation
The SESAM database represents the bridge between the UN resolutions and the Swiss legal system. When the sanctions committee modifies a list — adding or removing people, companies or organizations — the modification is immediately reported in SESAM and becomes binding on anyone operating in Switzerland. Banks, asset management companies, foreign trade companies and economic operators in general must verify customers and suppliers against the updated UN lists. On September 7, 2026, this verification became even more critical: the list has changed and any financial institution that does not update its controls risks serious violations. ### Automatic transposition and practical implications
The Federal Council's decision of 4 March 2016 represents a paradigm shift in the management of sanctions in Switzerland. Rather than wait for Parliament to legislate on each new UN measure, the Swiss government decided to delegate the power to update the lists directly to the UN Security Council. This approach reflects Switzerland's commitment to the multilateral system and to the fight against the financing of terrorism and illicit activities.
The operational consequence is immediate: no Swiss bank, no commercial company, no economic operator can claim not to be aware of a UN sanction. The September 7, 2026 amendment is effective as of September 7, 2026. Anyone who continues to transact with a sanctioned entity after that date commits a serious violation and becomes liable to administrative and criminal sanctions.
Each credit institution must implement automatic screening systems that compare its customers and suppliers against the updated SESAM database. The checks must take place: (1) at the time the commercial relationship is established; (2) periodically (at least monthly or quarterly); (3) immediately, as soon as a change is made public. A passive periodic check is not enough. Compliance requires active diligence and documentation of audits.
### What changes in the scope of sanctions
The UN list includes individuals, groups, businesses and international organizations believed to be linked to threats to international peace and security, terrorism, or weapons proliferation. The September 7, 2026 update changed this perimeter — although the official communication does not specify exactly which entities have been added or removed, every Swiss operator must assume that at least one change has occurred and act accordingly.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Concrete procedures: how to verify compliance
Economic operators and financial institutions must perform three levels of control. First level: initial verification when opening an account, establishing a business relationship or signing a contract. The new customer must be checked against SESAM before any transaction takes place. Second level: recurring periodic control. Most Swiss banks implement automatic monthly or quarterly screening. Third level: immediate reporting and blocking. If a match emerges, the bank must immediately freeze the funds, warn the customer (in certain cases) and report to the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) and the enforcement authorities.
Documentation of these checks is mandatory. Swiss supervisory authorities regularly inspect credit institutions to ensure compliance with compliance checks. A gap in verification — or blatant negligence — exposes the institution to significant administrative fines and, in extreme cases, to criminal prosecution for money laundering or violations of economic sanctions.
### Where to find SESAM and updates
The SESAM database is managed by the Swiss Federal Administration and publicly accessible online. Economic operators, legal consultants, financial sector professionals and banks connect directly to the portal to download and consult the updated lists. Each change, such as that of September 7, 2026, is made available in real time.
Furthermore, the Federal Council and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs issue official communications when important changes occur. Businesses that engage in international trade, manage foreign funds or have foreign clients must subscribe to automatic notifications from SESAM to be notified immediately of updates.

item.title: Rösti promises compensation for waste storage
item.description: Rösti presents the project for the Lägern Nord depot between Zurich and Aargau in Fisibach. Promised compensations, decision towards 2030, storage from 2050.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Rösti presents the Lägern Nord depot in Fisibach, over 400 people present - Deep deposit between AG and ZH in opaline clay, hundreds of meters deep - Promised compensation; CF decision ~2030, voting ~2030, storage by 2050
- **What**: Deep repository for radioactive waste (Lägern Nord) - When: CF decision ~2030, voting ~2030, storage from 2050 - Where: Lägern Nord (north-west Bülach), between cantons Zurich and Aargau - Who: Federal Councilor Albert Rösti (DETEC), Nagra, over 400 participants - Document: Nagra applied November 2024
### The Fisibach event
Albert Rösti, federal councilor and head of DETEC, appeared in Fisibach (Aargau) to illustrate the project for a deep repository for the safe storage of Swiss radioactive waste in front of over 400 people. The structure should be built in the Lägern Nord area, between the cantons of Zurich and Aargau.
During the meeting, Rösti assured the population of a "transparent, progressive and jointly conducted" approach and announced compensation for the region. He stressed that the safe disposal of radioactive waste is a national responsibility that cannot be delegated to future generations, with safety as the top priority. He also thanked the local population for taking on "an important project for the whole of Switzerland".
### The decision-making process towards 2050
The institutional path is complex and extends over several decades. The Federal Council should decide on the final choice of the site around 2030, considering the various objections received during the consultative phase. Subsequently, it will be up to Parliament to give its approval to the project.
Swiss direct democracy will have a crucial say: Rösti expects a popular vote around 2030. If approved by the people, the storage of the first radioactive waste should begin in 2050. This means that the project, although decided in the next few years, will not enter the operational phase for at least two decades. ### The Lägern Nord site: geology and precise location
The depot is planned to the north-west of Bülach, in the canton of Zurich, in a strategic position between the two cantons involved. The structure will descend hundreds of meters deep within a geological layer of opaline clay, chosen for its natural insulation properties and long-term stability.
The main access to the complex will be located in Stadel, canton of Zurich. However, the waste treatment facilities will not be built directly at the deep repository, but at the already existing intermediate repository in Würenlingen, Aargau. This geographical separation between the access location, the processing space and the deep storage reflects an optimization of logistics and safety processes dictated by national technical needs.
### Nagra and the federal administrative process
Responsibility for the entire project falls on the Cooperative Society for the Storage of Radioactive Waste (Nagra). In November 2024, Nagra submitted the official application for the construction of the depot to the Confederation, marking the formal start of the technical, administrative and political evaluation by the federal authorities.
Nagra's application represents the fruit of years of geological research and technical evaluations, culminating in the proposal for a site that combines safety requirements, geological stability and logistical feasibility. Approval by the Confederation (expected around 2030) will not be a formality: the Federal Council will have to assess the technical suitability of the site, the adequacy of the safety plans and the response to the objections raised by local communities and cantonal bodies.
### Next steps and the role of the population
The path to 2050 will be long and will require continuous dialogue between Nagra, the federal and cantonal authorities, and the interested population. Rösti confirmed that the process will be "conducted together with the population", indicating that local consultations will not be merely formal. Communities in Fisibach, Stadel, Würenlingen and surrounding areas will have the opportunity to express concerns during the federal consultation phases.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### The promised compensations: what will be defined
Rösti has announced compensation for the region affected by the project, but details regarding the amount, how it will be distributed and the specific beneficiaries have not yet been made public. This is a crucial issue for local communities: the presence of a national infrastructure of this kind brings national benefits but also territorial impacts such as land occupation, prolonged construction activities and long-term monitoring.
The compensations represent a recognition of this disparity: the Confederation recognizes that the cantons and municipalities concerned (Aargau and Zurich) support a project of national interest that does not generate immediate local economic benefits. Details on the composition, size and distribution of compensation will need to be negotiated and defined in the years leading up to the federal decision around 2030.
One of Rösti's key commitments was to emphasize the role of local people in decision-making. It guaranteed a "transparent, progressive and conducted together with the population" approach. This means that affected communities will not simply be informed ex post, but will have the opportunity to express concerns, criticisms and proposals during the consultative phases.
In Switzerland, federal decisions of this magnitude follow a principle of direct democracy involving both Parliament and citizens. The popular vote towards 2030 will be the crucial moment in which all Swiss will be able to express their opinion, not just residents of the affected cantons. This opens up broader debates on national responsibility for the nuclear waste cycle and on the fair sharing of infrastructure burdens.
### What to monitor in the coming years
Residents and cantonal authorities will need to remain active in the years leading up to 2030. The federal consultative process will seek feedback on safety, environmental, infrastructure and compensatory issues. The cantonal administrations of Zurich and Aargau will play a decisive role in collecting and transmitting the concerns of their citizens to the federal authorities.
Rösti's decision to visit Fisibach and promise compensation signals a recognition by the Confederation that local debate is legitimate and important for the overall success of the project. The next few years will be decisive in defining the exact contours of the deposit and its territorial implications.

item.title: IVF in Switzerland: Costs are not covered
item.description: In vitro fertilization costs up to 8,000 francs and is not reimbursed by KVG. One expert calls it "an injustice" because the WHO recognizes infertility as a disease.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - IVF costs up to 8'000 CHF and is not reimbursed by basic insurance - 50% of patients do not need IVF to conceive naturally - WHO recognizes infertility as a disease, but Switzerland does not cover it
## Key facts - **What**: In vitro fertilization not covered by KVG in Switzerland - Who: Fabien Murisier, director of the Medically Assisted Procreation Center (CPMA), Lausanne - Where: Lausanne and Switzerland - Amount: CHF 8'000 first cycle CHF 500-1'500 drugs - Percentage of patients without need for IVF: 50% - Statistics: Approximately 6,500 couples/year resort to reproductive medicine - Establishment: WHO recognizes infertility as a disease
In vitro fertilization is often the last option for those who are unable to have children naturally. In Switzerland, although infertility is recognized internationally as a disease, resorting to IVF involves an initial cost of around 8,000 francs. A cost that falls entirely on the patient's shoulders, without any guarantee of pregnancy and without reimbursement from basic insurance.
«An injustice», according to Fabien Murisier, director of the Center for Medically Assisted Procreation (CPMA) in Lausanne. "Reimbursing also means recognizing illness and suffering," underlined the expert.
### The path is partially covered
Every year in Switzerland around 6,500 couples turn to reproductive medicine. Yet not everyone necessarily needs to resort to in vitro fertilization. «Almost 50% of our patients manage to have a child without going through IVF», explains Murisier.
The healthcare system covers part of the reproductive path. Tests to understand the causes of infertility are reimbursed, as are some treatments: stimulation of ovulation for one year or up to three attempts at intrauterine insemination. For the other half of the patients, who must resort to IVF, the costs are entirely at their own expense. [Scopri la copertura LAMal per la medicina della riproduzione](nav:health).
### The real numbers of IVF
A first IVF costs around 8,000 francs, to which must be added between 500 and 1,500 francs for the necessary drugs. Failure does not mean having to start from scratch: IVF often allows you to obtain several embryos, and those not transferred immediately can be frozen for subsequent attempts. Each new transfer costs around 2,000 francs.
If the patient no longer has frozen embryos, she must repeat the entire procedure with all the associated costs. The final bill can vary greatly from one patient to the next, making it impossible to establish an average amount spent until the birth of a child. The WHO recognizes infertility as a disease, yet in Switzerland it remains completely the responsibility of the patient. ### Financial injustice and cultural taboo
It is precisely the variability of costs that makes the situation financially unfair. As Murisier points out, it is impossible to establish an average price for the complete journey up to birth. The mother's age has a huge impact on the outcome: the older she gets, the fewer embryos are obtained and the greater the risk of chromosomal anomalies. Some patients will get pregnant on the first transfer, others will need three or four attempts. This unpredictability makes the situation financially unfair and creates unacceptable inequalities in the right to access parenting.
In addition to the economic issue, the reimbursement would have an important symbolic value. Infertility remains surrounded by a certain cultural taboo in Switzerland, with the idea sometimes implied that the people affected are responsible for their own situation: too stressed or that it is enough to "leave it to nature". “The same would not be said for other diseases, such as cancer, for example,” underlines Murisier. Recognition through reimbursement would also mean dispelling this taboo and openly addressing the issue of infertility.
### The unequal treatment between heterosexual couples and female couples
There is a further difference in treatment in the Swiss healthcare system. If for a heterosexual couple with infertility problems some treatments are partially covered, for a couple made up of two women the situation is different. Health insurance companies generally believe that it is not infertility caused by illness and refuse to cover insemination with donor sperm.
«The vast majority of female couples we follow do not need IVF. In approximately 95% of cases we proceed with inseminations", specifies Murisier. Yet, precisely because those couples are not considered to be suffering from medical infertility, they remain without insurance coverage, creating a clear disparity in rights and access. 📊 This distinction reveals the inconsistency of the system: if infertility is a disease recognized by the WHO, the path to achieving a pregnancy — regardless of sexual orientation — should be treated the same way from an insurance point of view.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Where and how to contact
For those who live in Switzerland and find themselves in a situation of infertility, the first step is to consult your GP or a gynecologist for an evaluation. Diagnostic tests to identify the causes are generally covered by basic insurance, as are the first year of ovarian stimulation or up to three attempts at intrauterine insemination.
If these treatments do not bring results and the doctor believes that IVF is necessary, it is essential to be aware that the costs will not be covered. It is therefore necessary:
- Contact specialized facilities such as medically assisted procreation centers (CPMA) to obtain a realistic estimate of costs for your specific case - Contact your health insurance company to see which items may be partially covered - Check whether your KVG policy provides additional coverage which could include assisted reproduction
### Financial planning and options
According to Murisier and other experts, IVF reimbursement falls within the logic of inclusive healthcare that recognizes infertility as a disease and not as a personal choice. Although it is not currently covered by the Swiss basic insurance system, it is important to monitor political debates that could change this situation.
In the meantime, it is advisable to check whether some health insurance companies offer coverage for reproductive medicine. Each canton may also have specific guidelines for couples facing infertility issues. 💡 Disparities in costs and coverage make a personalized consultation with your insurance essential before embarking on an IVF process.
To better plan the financial implications and understand the various options available in your canton, compare the different Swiss health insurance companies and discover their coverage.

item.description: The security deposit may not exceed three months of rent; the dispute of the fee must take place within 30 days with the conciliation authority.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - Il diritto di locazione è federale (CO), uguale in ogni cantone - Deposito cauzionale massimo: 3 mesi di pigione - Contestazione del canone: entro 30 giorni all'autorità competente - La disdetta del locatore richiede forme specifiche e termini legali
## Fatti chiave - **Cosa**: Regole sul deposito cauzionale e contestazione canoni - Quando: Contestazione entro 30 giorni dalla consegna del modulo - Dove: Cantone di Ginevra e resto della Svizzera - Chi: Inquilini, locatori, autorità di conciliazione - Importo: Max 3 mesi di pigione per il deposito
Il mercato degli affitti nel Cantone di Ginevra si muove all'interno di un quadro giuridico rigorosamente definito a livello federale. La norma di riferimento è il Codice delle obbligazioni (CO), che stabilisce regole uniformi in tutta la Svizzera, indipendentemente dal cantone di residenza. Questo significa che un inquilino a Ginevra gode degli stessi diritti fondamentali di un inquilino a Zurigo o a Berna, garantendo una tutela standardizzata contro abusi nel settore immobiliare.
### Il deposito cauzionale: limite e gestione Uno dei punti più critici per chi si trasferisce è il deposito cauzionale. La legge federale impone un tetto rigido: il locatore non può chiedere più di tre mesi di pigione. Questo importo deve essere versato su un conto vincolato intestato specificamente all'inquilino, non al proprietario. Questa distinzione è cruciale: il denaro non entra nella disponibilità libera del locatore, ma resta separato e garantito. In caso di controversie al termine del contratto, il conto vincolato offre una tracciabilità immediata dei fondi, riducendo i rischi di litigi sul restituito. Per chi cerca un alloggio a Ginevra, dove la domanda spesso supera l'offerta, comprendere questo meccanismo permette di verificare immediatamente se le richieste del proprietario rispettino la soglia legale dei tre mesi.
La struttura del canone è anch'essa protetta. Il locatore non può aumentare la pigione a piacimento; qualsiasi modifica deve rispettare i criteri di ragionevolezza previsti dalla legge federale. Se un inquilino ritiene che il canone iniziale o un aumento successivo siano sproporzionati rispetto ai valori di mercato della zona, ha a disposizione uno strumento giuridico preciso: la contestazione formale. Non si tratta di una semplice lamentela verbale, ma di un atto procedurale che deve essere depositato presso l'autorità di conciliazione in materia di locazione. La tempistica è essenziale: la contestazione deve avvenire entro 30 giorni. Questo termine breve richiede reattività, ma offre alla controparte la possibilità di difendersi in un contesto paritario e non punitivo.
La disdetta del contratto segue regole analoghe di chiarezza e tempestività. Sebbene il diritto di locazione sia federale, la procedura di disdetta da parte del locatore deve rispettare termini precisi e forme scritte. La comunicazione non può essere informale; deve essere tracciabile e rispettare i preavvisi legali stabiliti dal contratto o dalla legge. In un mercato come quello ginevrino, dove la stabilità abitativa è un bene prezioso, la conoscenza di questi vincoli legali è la prima forma di protezione per l'inquilino. The practical analysis of federal rules in light of the Geneva reality reveals that legal standardization does not eliminate local differences, but channels them into clear procedures. Although the Code of Obligations is uniform, the application of norms regarding the reasonableness of rents varies based on the specific market values of each neighborhood. In Geneva, average rents can differ significantly between central and peripheral areas, but the principle of proportionality remains the same. The conciliation authority evaluates each case considering the type of property, its location, and current market conditions, rather than rigid national rules.
### Dispute and Conciliation Authority The dispute procedure is not an automatic path toward rent reduction, but a mandatory mediation phase before any appeal to the court. The conciliation authority for tenancy matters has the task of verifying whether the claimed rent complies with legal criteria. If the dispute is well-founded, the authority can order the reduction of the rent to the market value deemed fair. This mechanism protects the tenant from predatory increases, but requires solid documentation. Anyone intending to dispute a rent must be prepared to demonstrate that the requested rent exceeds reasonableness parameters. The 30-day timeframe is not extendable: a late dispute loses legal effect, leaving the tenant bound to the disputed rent.
For the landlord, the rules on termination are equally strict. The communication of termination must respect contractual and legal notice periods. In the absence of specific clauses, federal law establishes minimum notice periods that vary based on the duration of the contract. Written form is mandatory to guarantee the legal validity of the act. A verbal or informal termination has no legal value and cannot be invoked to terminate the contract. This formal requirement serves to prevent misunderstandings and to ensure that both parties are fully aware of the end of the tenancy relationship.
The practical impact of these norms on the cost of living in Geneva is significant. Transparency in termination and dispute procedures reduces uncertainty for those living in rented accommodation. The possibility to dispute a disproportionate rent within a short timeframe offers an immediate defense tool, preventing injustices from becoming entrenched over time. For families and workers moving to the Canton, understanding that tenancy law is federal eliminates the fear of incomprehensible or variable local regulations. Uniformity guarantees that rights are the same in every part of the country, facilitating mobility and long-term financial planning.
The management of the security deposit in a blocked account adds a further level of security. Since the account is in the tenant's name, the landlord cannot access the funds arbitrarily. In case of damage to the property, the landlord must prove the extent of the damage and request payment from the blocked account. This separation of assets reduces conflicts at the end of the contract, making the return process more straightforward and less subject to emotional disputes.

### Procedure for Dispute and Termination If you believe the rent is disproportionate, the dispute procedure must be initiated within 30 days of receiving the notice. The dispute document must be filed with the competent conciliation authority for the area where the property is located. It is advisable to attach supporting documentation, such as comparisons of similar rents in the same area. The authority will evaluate the case and propose a solution or record the decision. In case of disagreement, it is possible to proceed with an appeal to the civil court, but mediation is the mandatory first step.
For the termination of the contract, whether by the tenant or the landlord, the notice must be written and traceable. Registered mail or hand delivery with a receipt are the safest forms. Notice periods vary based on the duration of the contract and specific clauses; in the absence of other agreements, federal law establishes the legal minimums. Ignoring these terms can result in the termination being null and void, forcing the terminating party to maintain the contract until the next expiration date.
Checking the blocked account is an operation to be performed immediately after the deposit is paid. The tenant must receive confirmation that the account is registered in their name. item.title: Buying a house in the Canton of Geneva: prices and mortgage
item.description: Average prices in Geneva, own funds required, mortgage loan sustainability, transfer taxes and notary fees.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Geneva is among the most expensive residential markets in Switzerland - At least 20% of own funds is required for a mortgage - Transfer costs include cantonal tax and notary fees - The 33% rule guides the sustainability of the financing
## Key facts - **What**: guide to buying a home in Canton Geneva - When: reference scenario updated to 2026 - Where: Canton Geneva, Romandy - Who: resident buyers and new residents in Switzerland - Amount: minimum own funds recommended equal to 20% of the price - Ancillary cost: transfer and notary fees to be budgeted separately - Practical rule: annual housing expense within 33% of gross income
Buying a home in Canton Geneva means operating in one of the most expensive residential markets in the Confederation. The Genevan capital, located at the western end of the country, has recorded per-square-metre values among the highest in Switzerland for years, higher than those of Zurich, Bern, and Basel. Demand pressure, fueled by international institutions, multinationals, and a population with high spending capacity, sustains prices and makes financial planning particularly delicate.
The first pillar to consider is the share of own funds. Swiss banks apply consolidated prudential criteria: to obtain a second-rank mortgage (the so-called cascading mortgage, still widespread) or a first-rank mortgage, it is required that at least 20% of the purchase price be covered with unencumbered own capital. Part of these funds may come from the second and third pillar (LPP/BVG and pillar 3a), but early withdrawal rules vary and must be checked case by case. Below 20% of own funds the operation becomes difficult or requires special structures with higher costs.
### Mortgage sustainability The practical rule universally adopted by credit institutions is the so-called 33% rule: annual expenses related to the property — mortgage interest, amortization, and ancillary costs — must not exceed one-third of gross income. This parameter, shared by the Swiss Bankers Association (ASB/SBV), also guides credit granting in Geneva. It applies uniformly across the entire federal territory, since bank prudential discipline is regulated by federal rules. For beginners, it is worth simulating scenarios with higher interest rates than current ones, to verify the budget's resilience in the event of a rise in policy rates decided by the BNS/SNB. In addition to the purchase price, buyers in Geneva must budget a series of ancillary costs that can amount to several tens of thousands of francs. The most significant of these is the property transfer tax, governed by the cantonal tax law: it is applied to the market value of the property and its rate varies from canton to canton. In Geneva, it falls within a medium-to-high range compared to the rest of Switzerland. On top of this levy, buyers must factor in notary fees, land registry registration costs, and, where applicable, an intermediary commission if a real estate agency is used. As a rough guide, the sum of these ancillary costs is in the order of 3-5% of the purchase price, a share that must also be financed with own funds.
From a tax standpoint, real estate ownership in Switzerland generates three potential levels of taxation. The federal direct tax (IFD), administered by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV), applies to income and, in the case of rental of the property, to income from real estate assets. Cantonal and communal taxes are governed by the legislation of the Canton of Geneva, which sets rates and multipliers: each municipality applies its own multiplier to the cantonal tax, which means that the tax burden varies even between neighboring municipalities within the canton. For those buying as their primary residence and living there, specific reductions and deductions are available (including passive interest on mortgage debts), which must be claimed in the tax return.
### Comparisons and hypothetical scenarios Compared with buyers in German-speaking Switzerland, those buying in Geneva must on average allocate a larger share of their income to financing the property. A hypothetical scenario: a mid-range purchase, financed with 20% own funds and the remaining 80% through a mortgage, generates recurring costs (interest and amortization) that weigh more heavily on the family budget, simply because the purchase price is higher. The 33% rule still applies in the same way, but the amount to be repaid each year is larger. For this reason, simulating different rate scenarios is even more important in Geneva than elsewhere: a one-percentage-point change in the mortgage rate can translate into thousands of francs per year.
A second aspect to consider is risk coverage. Banks generally require that mortgage amortization be advanced by the age of 65 (men) or 64 (women), so that the debt is fully repaid before reaching the AVS/AHV retirement age. Occupational pension provision (LPP/BVG) may be drawn upon to build up the required own funds, but an early withdrawal reduces the future pension and must be weighed carefully.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step purchase procedure The buying process in Geneva usually follows these stages: assessment of personal financial capacity, gathering of documents (payslips, AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG statements, tax returns for the last three years), application for a pre-approval (so-called 'Finanzierungsbestätigung' or financing confirmation) from two or three lending institutions, property search through real estate portals or agencies, signing of a preliminary contract with payment of a deposit, attendance before the notary for the public deed, and registration in the Land Registry. Only after registration is ownership effectively transferred.
### Deadlines and practical aspects - Within 3 months of arriving in Switzerland: take out compulsory health insurance (LAMal/KVG), mandatory for every resident, including those who have just purchased a home. - **Permit verification**: foreign citizens holding a B or C permit can purchase a dwelling, but with restrictions on use (primary residence) and location (prohibitions in some tourist areas); G permit holders (cross-border commuters) face specific limitations, to be checked with the Canton. - Tax deduction period: mortgage interest can be deducted from taxable income on the tax return, within the limits set by federal and cantonal legislation.
### Useful tools To simulate the affordability of a mortgage and estimate the monthly instalment, it is worth using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which helps assess the impact of financing on net income. For those considering moving or comparing the cost of living between Cantons, the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) tool provides a useful comparative overview during the decision phase. Finally, to understand how much to allocate to the third pillar and optimise taxation, the guide to [pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) helps plan the maximum deductible contribution and its impact on the income tax return.

item.title: Nursery in Geneva: cantonal fees and subsidies
item.description: In Geneva kindergartens, day families and after-school have modulated rates on taxable income. Cantonal subsidies reduce the share borne by families.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Extra-family custody in Geneva: modulated rates on family taxable income - Cantonal subsidies available to reduce the actual cost of facilities - Nurseries, day families and after-school are part of the canton's official network - The application is submitted to the competent cantonal service before the start of the service
## Key facts - What * *: Cantonal childcare fee scheme based on income and family composition - When: Not yet specified in the source for the year of entry into force of the barème - Where: Canton of Geneva, recognized custodial facilities in the territory - Who: Resident families with children of custodial age, beneficiaries of cantonal subsidies - How it works: Progressive calculation linked to taxable income, with subsidies that reduce the share borne by the family - Types covered: Kindergartens, day families and after-school
The Canton of Geneva organizes the custody of children through a network of recognized structures — nurseries, day families and after-school services — whose cost for families is not fixed, but calculated with a progressive system linked to taxable income and the composition of the family unit. The declared objective of the cantonal tariff mechanism is to make custody accessible also to families with medium-low incomes, modulating economic participation on the basis of effective contributory capacity.
The calculation of the The logic of the Geneva model reflects a principle widespread throughout the Confederation: childcare is considered a service of public interest, and its funding combines family participation with subsidiary intervention by public authorities. The income-based sliding-scale tariff prevents the cost of childcare from becoming a barrier to employment for families with young children, a topic also central to federal debates on female employment and the cost of living.
In practical terms, two families with children of the same age, living in the same neighbourhood and enrolled in the same facility may pay very different amounts. The difference depends entirely on declared taxable income and family composition. A single-earner family with one child enrolled full-time in a nursery will have its contribution calculated on disposable income after deductions, while a dual-earner household will be placed in a higher tariff bracket, for the same number of childcare hours.
### Comparison between the three childcare arrangements The three main forms of extrafamilial childcare recognised in Geneva meet different needs and have different hidden costs for the community. The nursery (asilo nido) welcomes pre-school-age children with qualified educational staff and generally extended hours. Day family care (famille de jour) offers care in a family setting, with a limited number of children and more flexible hours. The after-school care (parascolaire) is intended for school-age children and covers the afternoon slots.
From the perspective of family finances, the cantonal subsidy reduces net expenditure in inverse proportion to income: the lower the taxable income, the higher the share covered by the subsidy. The mechanism makes the cost of childcare comparable, proportionally, between families in different income brackets, even though the absolute figure remains different.
### Hypothetical calculation scenario Let us assume a family with two children enrolled in a nursery and an after-school programme. The household taxable income places the family in a middle tariff bracket. The daily rate charged by the facility is not paid in full by the family: the cantonal subsidy covers the difference between the full cost of the service and the share borne by the parents as determined by the sliding scale. The result is a lower monthly childcare expenditure than the same family would face in the absence of the progressive mechanism.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). To access the reduced tariff regime and cantonal subsidies for childcare in Geneva, resident families must follow a precise procedure, managed entirely by the cantonal administration. The application must be submitted before the start of the service at the designated cantonal counter, which verifies the requirements and calculates the applicable rate.
### Step-by-step application procedure The first step consists of gathering income and family documentation: recent tax return, certification of household members, and proof of residence in the Canton of Geneva. The second step is choosing a childcare facility recognized by the canton — nurseries, day families, or after-school care — and agreeing on the attendance calendar and schedule with them.
The third step involves submitting the subsidy application to the competent cantonal office, attaching the documentation collected and the contract or enrollment confirmation with the facility. The cantonal administration calculates the applicable rate based on taxable income and family composition, and communicates to the family the amount of the share to be paid and the extent of the subsidy.
The fourth step concerns payment: the family pays the facility only the share determined by the cantonal calculation, while the subsidy is paid directly to the facility or to the family according to the methods provided by the canton. Any significant change in family income or household composition must be communicated promptly for the rate to be redetermined.
### Deadlines and updates The tariff regime and subsidy criteria are periodically updated by the canton. Families already receiving benefits must submit an annual income declaration to maintain the right to the reduced rate. Failure to meet deadlines may result in the restoration of the full rate until the situation is regularized.

item.title: Scholarships in the Canton of Geneva: requirements and amounts
item.description: Scholarships and study loans in the Canton of Geneva: merit and income requirements, maximum amounts, terms and competent cantonal office.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Grants and loans are managed at the cantonal level, based on merit and income criteria - Maximum amounts vary according to the level of education and family situation - Applications are submitted online before the start of the academic year - The competent office is the Service des bourses et prêts d'études of the Canton of Geneva
## Key facts - **What**: Study grants and loans for students residing in the Canton of Geneva - When: Applications must be submitted before the start of the academic year; specific annual deadlines - Where: Canton of Geneva, addressed to the Service des bourses et prêts d'études - Who: Eligible students according to the cantonal law on study grants (LBSE) - Amount: Maximum amounts calculated on the basis of tuition fees, living/accommodation costs, and family situation; exact figures reviewed annually - Legal reference: Cantonal law on study grants and loans (Loi sur les bourses et prêts d'études, LBSE) and its implementing regulations - Deadline: Annual deadlines published on the official website of the Canton
Financial aid for education in Switzerland is a cantonal responsibility. Each Canton — including Geneva — defines by its own law the requirements, amounts, and procedures for obtaining study grants and loans. The Canton of Geneva regulates the matter through the LBSE (Loi sur les bourses et prêts d'études), which sets the cumulative conditions of academic merit and family income for accessing the subsidy.
The competent cantonal office is the Service des bourses et prêts d'études, rattaché au Département de l'instruction publique (DIP). Applications are submitted electronically through the dedicated cantonal portal. The procedure assesses two dimensions: on the one hand, the financial situation of the parents (or of the student themselves if independent), and on the other, academic results and the type of education undertaken.
### Who can apply
Applications may be submitted by adult students enrolled in a recognized post-compulsory education (vocational baccalaureate, gymnasial baccalaureate, university of applied sciences, university, university of teacher education) at a recognized Swiss or foreign institution. The LBSE also provides the possibility of applying for a study loan, repayable on favorable terms, potentially complementary to the grant.
For cross-border students — who in Switzerland generally fall under the G permit — different rules apply: financial aid for education is typically reserved for those whose tax residence is in the Canton. Holders of a B permit (residence) and C permit (settlement) may also in principle access it, provided that the education is followed at a recognized Swiss institution and the income and merit criteria are met. ## How the grant amount is calculated
The grant amount is not a fixed figure: it is determined by the difference between the recognized costs of education (enrolment fees, food, accommodation, teaching materials, transport) and the financial contribution considered reasonable from the family. The lower the parents' taxable income and assets, the higher the grant, up to the cantonal ceiling.
The Canton reassesses the maximum amounts and income thresholds every year. To avoid incorrect amounts, it is advisable to consult the website of the Service des bourses et prêts d'études each year: there you will find the updated caps per type of training, the table of deductions for dependent children and the income brackets. Large families or those with children already at university benefit from higher allowances, because the calculation takes into account the number of dependent persons.
### Grant, loan or both
The LBSE distinguishes between study grants (non-repayable) and study loans (to be repaid after the end of studies, at a preferential rate and with an instalment plan). Some students receive only the grant, others only the loan, and others a combination of the two. The choice depends on the cantonal assessment of the residual financial need.
At national level, the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Directors of Public Education (CDIP) coordinates minimum standards between Cantons. This does not unify the amounts, but it ensures that no deserving and needy student is excluded solely on the grounds of domicile. For Ticinese residents and Swiss nationals moving to Geneva to study, this means that the grant follows the Canton of fiscal domicile — not the Canton of origin.
### Cost of living comparison
Studying in Geneva has one of the highest costs of living in Switzerland: rents for a student room are in the upper range of the Swiss market, and the LAMal health insurance premiums are among the highest in the country. The grant calculation takes these real parameters into account: for a student living away from home in an independent flat, the theoretical maximum grant will be higher than for a student still living with their parents.
### Taxation and family impact
The Canton of Geneva applies the direct federal tax (IFD) on the income and assets of individuals, added to the cantonal and municipal tax with its own multiplier. Study grants received under the LBSE are exempt from direct federal tax — a point often overlooked by families. For AVS/AHV pensions and LPP/BVG benefits, on the other hand, there is no direct interaction with the grant: these are social security benefits relating to old age, not to education.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Step-by-step procedure
The procedure for applying for a scholarship in Geneva follows a precise sequence. Here is how to proceed.
### 1. Check the basic requirements
Before opening your application, make sure you meet the three cumulative conditions: being enrolled (or about to enrol) in a recognised post-compulsory education programme; having tax domicile in the Canton of Geneva (or effective residence for the cases provided for by the LBSE); having a family income level below the applicable cantonal thresholds.
### 2. Gather the documents
You will typically need: certificate of enrolment at the school or university, parents' tax return (or the student's own if independent), salary certificate, statement of any other scholarships or loans, proof of family situation (dependent children, separations, widowhood). Holders of B or C permits must also attach a copy of the permit and proof of domicile.
### 3. Online submission
The application is submitted via the Canton of Geneva's eBourse portal. It is possible to start the procedure before the beginning of the academic year, in order to speed up the disbursement. The ordinary deadline usually falls in the summer months (July-September) for the following academic year; the exact dates are published on the website of the Service des bourses et prêts d'études.
### 4. Follow-up and decision
After submission, the cantonal office reviews the file and may request additional documents. The decision is communicated by post, indicating the amount granted (scholarship, loan or both), the duration and the obligations for annual renewal. In the event of a rejection, there is a right of appeal with specific deadlines indicated in the communication.
### 5. Renewal and transfers
The scholarship must be renewed every academic year with proof of continued studies and an update of the family's income situation. Anyone who changes Canton during their studies must resubmit the application to the new Canton of tax domicile.
### Deadlines not to forget
There are two key deadlines: the date of submission of the initial application (so as not to lose the reference year) and the deadline for appeal in the event of a negative decision. Missing the first deadline means waiting until the following year; missing the second one precludes administrative contestation.
For those planning the family budget, it is worth simulating in advance the impact of a scholarship — even just a theoretical one — on disposable income. Our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) lets you estimate the monthly net amount taking into account AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG contributions and taxes, so you can compare the actual weight of the different sources of funding during the years of study.

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Geneva
item.description: Dual path in Geneva: internship contract, salary, professional maturity and access to the SUP. Complete guide.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Apprenticeship in Switzerland: three- or four-year pathway - Dual training: vocational school + host company - Vocational baccalaureate: access to Universities of Applied Sciences - Canton of Geneva: cantonal offices for vocational training
## Key facts - **What**: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Geneva - When: Not yet specified - Where: Canton of Geneva, Switzerland - Who: Cantonal offices for vocational training of the Canton of Geneva - How to find a position: Apply to recognised host companies - Contract: Training contract between apprentice and host company - Remuneration: Apprentice's salary according to cantonal directives and the sector - Vocational baccalaureate: Qualification that grants access to Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS)
## Vocational training in the Canton of Geneva
The Swiss vocational training system is one of the cornerstones of the national labour market, and the Canton of Geneva is an integral part of it. Initial vocational training in Switzerland is structured as a dual pathway that combines theoretical teaching at a vocational school with practical training at a recognised host company. This model, unique in the European landscape, ensures young people direct entry into the working world.
In Switzerland, vocational training is regulated at the federal level by the Vocational Training Act (LFPr). The Canton of Geneva, like all other cantons, is responsible for applying this legislation within its territory and has its own cantonal offices dedicated to managing and supervising training pathways. The cantonal offices for vocational training of the Canton of Geneva support trainees, host companies and vocational schools throughout the entire pathway.
### How to find an apprenticeship position
Searching for an apprenticeship position in Geneva follows the same dynamics as in the rest of Switzerland. Host companies publish apprenticeship offers directly or through employment services. The cantonal offices for vocational training provide support with career guidance and in finding an apprenticeship position, as well as coordinating orientation internships and enrolment procedures at vocational schools. Families and young people can contact these cantonal services to obtain up-to-date information on the professions available in the canton. ## The training contract and apprentice remuneration
The training contract is the formal act by which a training company undertakes to train an apprentice and the latter undertakes to follow the trainer's instructions. In Switzerland the training contract is regulated by the Vocational Education and Training Act (LFPr/VET Act) and the Code of Obligations (CO/OR). Working conditions — working hours, holidays, salary — are governed by federal labour legislation. The maximum working time is 45 hours per week for the industrial, office and sales sectors, and 50 hours per week for the other sectors. Minimum holidays are 4 weeks per year (5 weeks for apprentices under the age of 20).
### Apprentice remuneration
Apprentice remuneration varies according to the year of training and the professional sector. In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage, but the Canton of Geneva has its own minimum wage provisions, which also apply to apprentices. Apprentice remuneration is also influenced by collective employment contracts (CCL/CCT) when the sector provides for one. Social contributions on apprentice wages follow the same rules applicable to other employees in Switzerland.
### The vocational maturity (maturità professionale)
The federal vocational maturity (Berufsmaturität / maturité professionnelle) is a qualification obtained at the end of a three- or four-year vocational education programme, by completing a parallel general education. This qualification gives access to the Universities of Applied Sciences (SUP/FH) and, under certain conditions, to the Universities of Teacher Education (ASP/PH) and other tertiary-level programmes. The vocational maturity is a different track from the gymnasial maturity, which instead prepares students for direct access to the federal universities and the ETH/EPF. In the Canton of Geneva, vocational schools offer preparatory courses for the vocational maturity during or shortly after the apprenticeship.
## Comparison between education pathways in Switzerland
The Swiss education system offers two main pathways at the end of compulsory schooling. On one side, dual vocational education, leading to a federal vocational certificate (AFC/CFC) or to a federal certificate of practical education (CFP/CFPC), which can be completed with the vocational maturity. On the other side, gymnasial education, leading to the gymnasial maturity and access to universities. Vocational education represents the choice of the majority of young Swiss people, and is internationally recognised for its ability to integrate theory and practice.
## Labour market data and social security
For those starting an apprenticeship in Switzerland, it is useful to know certain aspects relating to the labour market and social security. The Swiss labour market is monitored by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO). Labour market and median wage statistics are published by the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS). As regards social security, AVS/AHV contributions are deducted from the wage even for apprentices, at the ordinary rates. The Federal Law on the Transfer of Pension Benefits (LFLP/FZG) and the Occupational Pensions Act (LPP/BVG) apply to employment relationships subject to the LPP/BVG, according to the salary thresholds set by federal regulations.
## Practical implications for those choosing an apprenticeship in Geneva
Choosing an apprenticeship in the Canton of Geneva has practical implications at the tax and insurance level. Apprentice wages are subject to federal direct tax (IFD), cantonal tax, and communal tax. In Switzerland the tax system provides for three levels: federal, cantonal and communal. Each canton has its own tax law and each municipality applies a multiplier on the cantonal tax. Health insurance under the LAMal/KVG (Federal Health Insurance Act) is compulsory for all residents in Switzerland and must be taken out within three months of arrival. The same residence and work permit provisions apply to apprentices coming from abroad.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to proceed concretely for an apprenticeship in the Canton of Geneva
### Step 1 — Career guidance and choice of profession
The first step consists in exploring the available professions and one's own inclinations. The Canton of Geneva has career guidance services that help young people identify the professions best suited to their profile. These services are managed at cantonal level and are free of charge.
### Step 2 — Searching for an apprenticeship position
The search for an apprenticeship position can be carried out through training companies, employment offices or the official website of the Canton of Geneva dedicated to vocational education and training. Recognised training companies publish vacancies according to the needs of the sector.
### Step 3 — Signing the apprenticeship contract
The apprenticeship contract is concluded between the apprentice (or their legal representatives if a minor) and the training company. The contract must indicate the duration of the apprenticeship, the remuneration, the holidays, the working hours and the training objectives. In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage, but the Canton of Geneva may have its own cantonal minimum wage that also applies to apprentices. The apprentice's remuneration is also defined by the relevant sectoral collective labour agreement (CCL), where applicable.
### Step 4 — Enrolment at the vocational school
In parallel with the signing of the contract, the apprentice is enrolled at a vocational school recognised by the canton. The vocational school provides the theoretical part of the training. Lessons are generally held one or two days a week, with the rest of the time devoted to practical training in the company.
### Step 5 — Insurance and social security
The apprentice is covered by the Swiss social insurances: AVS/AHV, AI, IPG. Compulsory health insurance under the LAMal/KVG must be taken out within three months of the start of the employment relationship or of arrival in Switzerland. SUVA provides insurance against occupational and non-occupational accidents.
### Step 6 — Obtaining the certificate and the vocational baccalaureate
At the end of the apprenticeship, the apprentice undergoes a qualification procedure leading to the award of the federal certificate of capacity (CFC/AFC) or the federal certificate of practical training (AFP/CFP). At the same time or subsequently, the apprentice may prepare the federal vocational baccalaureate, which opens the doors of the Universities of Applied Sciences (HES/SUP).
## Deadlines and administrative aspects
Apprenticeship positions in the Canton of Geneva are generally published well in advance of the start of the training. Enrolment at vocational schools takes place through the cantonal offices. For non-Swiss foreign nationals, the conditions of access depend on the residence permit. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) is the federal authority responsible for permits.
To learn more about the tax and salary aspects related to an apprenticeship in Switzerland, the tools available on the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) can be consulted. For those actively looking for an apprenticeship or a job in Switzerland, the [job listings](nav:jobs) section collects the latest offers.

item.title: School system in the Canton of Geneva: cycles, enrolment and calendar
item.description: How compulsory school works in Geneva: cycles, enrolment age, teaching languages and transition to high school.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Geneva's public school system covers compulsory education through cycles organised by age group - Teaching is predominantly in French, with English introduced in the later cycles - Enrolment takes place through the cantonal service responsible for resident families - The transition from the final cycle to upper secondary schools follows established cantonal criteria
## Key facts - **What**: Organisation of compulsory public schooling in the Canton of Geneva - When: School year defined by the cantonal calendar (specific dates not indicated in the source) - Where: Canton of Geneva, French-speaking Switzerland - Who: Cantonal Department of Public Education (Département de l'instruction publique, DIP) - Cost: not yet specified in the source (school fees in cantonal public schools are generally free for compulsory schooling) - Languages: French as the main language of instruction; English and German as second languages - Structure: Successive cycles (cycle élémentaire, cycle moyen, cycle d'orientation) - Compulsion: Compulsory schooling for cantonal residents, according to federal and cantonal legislation
The public school system in the Canton of Geneva is organised into progressive cycles covering the entire span of compulsory education. Unlike other Swiss cantons, which refer to 'primary school' and 'secondary school', the Geneva model groups the school years into three distinct cycles, each with specific pedagogical objectives and variable duration. This structure reflects the approach of the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (CDIP/EDK), which coordinates minimum standards at national level through the HarmoS agreement.
### Enrolment and admission
Enrolment in the public school system is managed by the Département de l'instruction publique (DIP) of the Canton of Geneva. For families moving into the canton, the procedure involves registering with the school service of the municipality of residence and submitting identity documents and the previous school record. Children of compulsory school age who are residents are assigned to the school in their district, unless exemptions apply for specific reasons (health, proximity to the parents' workplace, the facility's capacity). Linguistic transition pathways are provided for children whose mother tongue is not French.
### School calendar
The Geneva school year follows the calendar defined by the DIP, generally starting in August-September and divided into semesters with autumn, winter, Carnival and spring breaks. The exact dates of school holidays are published year by year by the canton; for details of the current year, it is necessary to consult the official calendar published by the Département de l'instruction publique.
### Transition to upper secondary schools
At the end of the cycle d'orientation, pupils are guided towards upper secondary schools (collège, école de culture générale, vocational school) based on the competences acquired, the aptitudes demonstrated and the educational project. Guidance is a process involving teachers, the family and counselling services. ### Comparison with other cantons
The cycle system adopted in Geneva differs from that of other Swiss cantons. In German-speaking cantons, for example, the typical scan is “Primarschule” (primary school) followed by “Sekundarstufe I” (lower secondary school) with differentiated levels (Realschule, Sekundarschule, Bezirksschule or Gymnasium). In Geneva, the division into cycles instead groups the primary and lower secondary arches under a single pedagogical direction, attenuating — at least formally — the separation between the two moments.
This choice reflects the pedagogical will to avoid early labelling of students. In fact, the cycle model aims to evaluate skills in progress, distributing orientation decisions over several years. In cantons with strong differentiation of levels from the 7th to the 8th year, separation occurs at an earlier age.
### Languages of teaching and multilingualism
French is the language of instruction in the Canton of Geneva, consistent with its location in French-speaking Switzerland. English is the first foreign language introduced, followed by German at a later stage. The cantonal objective is the learning of at least two second languages in addition to the mother tongue.
For children of parents from other cantons or abroad, the system provides for reception devices and transition classes dedicated to intensive learning of school French.
### New Families
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Practical procedure to enrol a child
**Step 1 — Civil registration.** The family registers their residence with the residents' registration office (contrôle des habitants) of the Geneva municipality where they intend to settle. Without a residence certificate, it is not possible to start the schooling procedure.
Step 2 — Contact with the school service. Once the residence certificate has been obtained, the family contacts the school secretariat of their district or the DIP central service to begin the enrolment process. It is advisable to attend with civil registration documents and the previous school record (if available).
Step 3 — Assessment and assignment to a cycle. The school service checks the pupil's age and previous schooling, then assigns the class corresponding to the appropriate cycle. For non-Francophone children, a language assessment is provided, with possible placement in transition programmes.
Step 4 — School calendar and timetables. The family receives the calendar for the current school year, with start dates, holidays and administrative deadlines. Timetables and the organisation of school days are defined by each individual institution within the cantonal framework.
Step 5 — Transition between cycles. At the end of each cycle, the family takes part in review meetings organised by the school. Progression to the next cycle is automatic unless the class council decides otherwise with due justification.
Step 6 — Guidance to upper secondary education. In the final year of the orientation cycle, the family and the pupil are supported through the guidance process towards the collège, the école de culture générale or vocational training.
### Useful documents to consult
For up-to-date calendars, enrolment forms and detailed information on the cycles, the official reference is the website of the Département de l'instruction publique of the Canton of Geneva. Municipalities also publish contact details for the district school secretariats.
For those moving from another Swiss canton, it is advisable to request the so-called 'certificat de scolarité' (schooling certificate) or a similar document from the previous school, confirming the class attended and the skills acquired: it makes it easier to place the child in the appropriate cycle.

## In brief - Family and education allowances in the Canton of Geneva - Monthly amounts established for each dependent child - Entitlement conditions governed by local regulations - Application to be submitted through the competent compensation fund
## Key facts - **What**: Family and education allowances - Where: Canton of Geneva - Competence: Competent compensation fund - Recipients: Families with eligible children - Payment: Monthly disbursement based on requirements
Within the landscape of Swiss social benefits, the family allowances system represents a fundamental pillar for the support of family units residing or working in the various cantons. Focusing on the Canton of Geneva, the legislation provides specific economic measures intended to partially cover the maintenance costs of children. These measures include both the allowance for minor children and the education allowance for young people who continue their studies or vocational training beyond compulsory school age. The management of these benefits is carried out through specialised bodies that strictly apply the criteria established by the current cantonal provisions. Every employee or person without gainful activity who meets the legal requirements may submit the application to benefit from the monthly subsidy. The amount varies depending on the category of benefit and the age of the recipient, ensuring economic support calibrated to the actual needs of the family. The Swiss administrative organisation provides that the application is carefully examined to verify the existence of all the legal prerequisites necessary before the actual disbursement of the established funds.
### Basic conditions for accessing benefits In order to access family allowances in the Canton of Geneva, it is necessary to meet specific legal requirements concerning residence, work activity, or status as a person without gainful activity. The legislation establishes that the right belongs primarily to the person who carries out a dependent or independent gainful activity. In the event that both parents carry out a work activity or are in the condition of not having one, federal and cantonal rules of precedence apply to determine which parent should receive the main allowance. It is also essential that the child resides permanently in Switzerland or, under certain conditions provided for by international or bilateral agreements, abroad if specific reciprocity agreements exist. The verification of the contribution and employment situation constitutes the first essential step to avoid double payments or disputes between different compensation funds. The offices in charge carry out periodic checks to ensure that the requirements remain unchanged over time, especially during the periods of scholastic or professional transition of the dependent children. The practical analysis of the procedures and mechanisms for paying family allowances in the Canton of Geneva requires attention to local specificities compared to other Swiss contexts. Compensation funds play a central role in the daily interaction with employers and individual applicants. For employees, it is normally the employer who handles the transmission of documentation to the relevant compensation fund, including the amount due directly in the monthly [pay slip](nav:payslip). Conversely, self-employed workers and persons without gainful activity must deal directly with the competent body to present their situation and request payment of the amounts owed. This procedural distinction directly affects processing times and the need to produce updated certificates, such as school attendance certificates for young people attending upper secondary schools or apprenticeship courses.
### Compensation funds and administrative management The Genevan administrative structure relies on professional, company-level, or cantonal compensation funds authorized to manage the family allowances branch. The Cantonal Compensation Fund represents the main point of reference for self-employed professionals and for those who do not fall within category-specific professional funds. Any change in family situation, such as the birth of a new child, a change of employment, separation, or reaching the age limit for studies, must be promptly communicated to the paying body. Failure to report changes in a timely manner may result in unfavorable adjustments or requests for repayment of amounts unduly received. For those who manage their own accounting or evaluate the overall family budget, understanding how these deductions and benefits work alongside general social contributions such as [AVS/AHV](nav:pension) helps maintain a clear view of monthly net income and allows for more precise planning of household expenses.

The procedure for submitting a family allowance application in the Canton of Geneva follows a formalized process that requires filling out specific forms provided by the competent authority. Applicants must gather a series of essential documents, including the child's birth certificate, civil status certificates, and, in the case of education allowances, proof of regular enrollment in a recognized educational institution. For employees, the application form is usually submitted to the employer, who will forward it to the relevant company or professional compensation fund. For self-employed workers or persons without gainful activity, the complete dossier must be sent directly to the cantonal fund or designated institution.
### Deadlines and periodic verifications It is essential to respect the statutory deadlines set for retroactive claims, as in Switzerland the right to back payments is generally limited to a maximum period established by federal and cantonal provisions, often set at five years. Once the right has been obtained, families must pay attention to annual or semi-annual deadlines linked to the submission of school certificates, especially for young people who exceed the minimum compulsory school age.
