## Briefly - Issued for stays of less than one year - Strictly tied to the initial employment contract - Managed by the competent authorities of the Canton of Geneva - Possible verification of requirements in case of extension
## Key Facts - **What**: Short-term L permit - Where: Canton of Geneva - Duration: Up to one year according to SEM provisions - Restrictions: Tied to the employer's conditions - Renewal: Subject to specific cantonal evaluations
The short-term L permit represents a fundamental tool within the regulatory framework of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) to regulate the presence of foreign citizens on Swiss territory in general, and in the Canton of Geneva in particular. This authorization is issued to cover temporary employment needs, the total duration of which generally does not exceed the limit of one calendar year. The entire application and issuance procedure is based on federal provisions applied by the competent cantonal offices, which verify the existence of a valid employment contract compliant with local professional and salary standards currently in force in the Geneva region.
### Reference Legislation and Cantonal Authorities
The management of temporary residence authorizations falls to the cantonal bodies in close coordination with the federal directives established by the SEM. In the Canton of Geneva, anyone intending to settle temporarily for professional reasons must submit complete documentation to the competent authority. The L permit does not automatically guarantee a right to conversion into a higher-category residence permit, such as the B permit, although under certain circumstances and following a thorough evaluation of employment and personal stability, new prospects for long-term stay may open up in the national and cantonal context. The practical analysis of the implications connected to holding an L permit in the Canton of Geneva requires an in-depth understanding of the administrative and professional constraints that characterize this residence permit. Unlike more stable authorizations, the short-term permit is designed to respond to cyclical needs or time-limited fixed-term mandates. This specificity is directly reflected in the worker's position regarding the local labor market and the cantonal authorities responsible for controlling the entry and stay of foreigners.
### Constraints related to the employer and mobility
One of the central aspects of the L permit concerns the direct link with the employment relationship authorized at the time of issuance. Any substantial changes to employment conditions, including early termination of the contract or a change of duties and employer, must be promptly communicated and, in cases provided for by current provisions, subjected to a new authorization by the competent Geneva offices. This regulation protects the standards of the Swiss labor market, preventing distortions and ensuring compliance with federal and cantonal regulations regarding wages and social security.
### Related tax and social security aspects
During the period of validity of the L permit, the worker is subject to the tax and contribution obligations established by the Swiss system. Depending on the specific situation, if the worker actually resides in the Canton of Geneva, withholding taxes or ordinary taxation regimes apply, in addition to mandatory contributions for social security (AVS/AI/IPG) and LAMal coverage regarding mandatory health insurance to be taken out within the established deadlines. Before the natural expiry of the permit, usually set within twelve months, it is essential to verify whether the conditions exist to request an extension or if the work activity is coming to an end, requiring the conclusion of the stay or conversion to another type of permit provided for by the federal SEM legislation.

1. Verify the expiry date indicated on the residence document issued by the Geneva authorities. 2. item.title: Naturalization in Thurgau: requirements, tests and procedure
item.description: How to obtain citizenship in the Canton of Thurgau: years of residence, language, tests and costs.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C and 10 years of residence in Switzerland for ordinary naturalization - In Thurgau you also need years of domicile in the canton and municipality - Mandatory language and integration tests before application - Cantonal and municipal taxes: amounts vary, check on the municipality's website
## Key facts - **What**: Ordinary naturalization procedure in the canton of Thurgau - Who: Foreign residents with C permit, according to cantonal law - Where: Canton Thurgau, with cantonal office and municipal authorities - Federal requirement: Permit C + 10 years of residence in Switzerland (years 8–18 count double) - Cantonal requirement: Years of residence in the canton (Thurgau) and in the municipality, to be verified on a case-by-case basis - Tests: Language and integration, mandatory - Taxes: Variable amounts at cantonal and municipal level (not yet specified in this guide) - Duration: Multi-level procedure (cantonal + municipal), times not uniquely quantified
Obtaining Swiss citizenship is a shared competence between the Confederation, Canton and Municipality. For those who live in the canton of Thurgau, the ordinary naturalization procedure follows the Federal Law on Swiss Citizenship and the Thurgau cantonal legislation. The first stake, set in Bern, is the possession of residence permit C, issued by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) after a certain period of regular stay.
### Who can apply for naturalization ### What changes compared to other Cantons
Every Swiss canton has its own citizenship law and its own fee level, and this makes the Thurgau procedure different from those of Zurich, Bern or Vaud, just to give a few examples. While the federal requirement (C permit + 10 years, of which the years between 8 and 18 count double) is identical for everyone, the cantons add their own hurdles, usually linked to language skills and social integration.
In Thurgau, as in many other German-speaking Swiss cantons, the required language is German, at a level that is verified through a standard test. For those coming from a German-speaking region, this aspect is marginal; for those coming from other linguistic regions, it is instead a crucial turning point. The integration test, for its part, covers basic knowledge of the Swiss system, political rights, history and daily life.
### Real and cumulative costs
The naturalization fee in Switzerland is made up of three items: the federal fee (set by the Federal Migration Office), the Thurgau cantonal fee and the fee of the municipality of residence. The federal fee is the same across the whole national territory; the cantonal and municipal ones vary. Added to these are the costs of any language courses, preparation materials, and, if one uses a consultancy service, professional fees.
To avoid unpleasant surprises, it is advisable to ask for a detailed quote from the chancery of the municipality of residence, which will be able to provide the exact amount of the local fees in force. The same applies to the cantonal stage.
### Practical process: three levels, three steps
The procedure is structured similarly in all cantons, but with local nuances that matter. In Thurgau one starts with the cantonal application: collection of documents, proof of language, verification of integration requirements. Once the cantonal preliminary opinion has been obtained, the application passes to the municipality, where the local authority assesses the person's integration into community life. For municipalities that provide for a vote in assembly, the application is discussed publicly. Once this step has been passed, the Confederation issues the citizenship certificate and the person becomes a Swiss citizen.
### Timelines: how long it really takes
The timing of the procedure varies according to the workload of the bodies involved and the completeness of the documentation. A well-prepared application, with all the correct documents, can be handled in reasonable time; a patchy file risks lengthening the times due to requests for integration. There is no single deadline valid for all Thurgau municipalities: each stage has its own schedule.
### Possible obstacles and how to avoid them
The reasons for refusal can be of various kinds: insufficient knowledge of the language, criminal record, behaviour contrary to public order, dependence on social assistance, or interruption of the integration path. To reduce the risk, it is advisable to prepare well in advance: improve German, take part in the life of the municipality, regularize one's tax and contribution position.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step: how to proceed in practice
Anyone planning to start the naturalisation procedure in Thurgau can follow a concrete path, to be adapted to their municipality of residence.
1. Check the basic requirements. First of all, make sure you hold a C permit and have completed the years of residence required at federal level. Years spent in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 count double.
**2. Gather documents.** Passport, residence permit, employment certificates, language certificates, criminal record certificate, and any other document required by the municipal clerk's office or the cantonal office.
3. Language test. Register for a recognised German exam, if German is not your mother tongue. In the Canton of Thurgau, the required level is defined by cantonal law.
4. Cantonal application. Submit the application to the competent cantonal office, along with all documentation and payment of the cantonal fee.
5. Municipal application. After cantonal approval, the application moves to the municipality, which may involve an assembly vote.
6. Federal decision. Final step: the Confederation, based on the cantonal and municipal outcomes, issues the citizenship certificate.
### Typical documents to prepare
- Valid identity document - Valid C residence permit - Language certificate (German) at the required level - Residence and stay certificates - Any criminal record or pending charges certificates - Proof of sufficient financial means - Integration certificates (work, volunteering, participation)
### Mistakes to avoid
Underestimating the municipal stage is one of the most common mistakes: even with a flawless cantonal process, the municipality can reject the application for local reasons. Another frequent mistake is submitting incomplete documentation, which extends the timelines. Finally, forgetting to update personal data (change of address, marital status) can create issues during the verification phase.
### Useful tools on the site
For those preparing for naturalisation, it can be useful to simulate the tax impact of a change of status or assess the social contributions involved. The site provides a calculator that allows you to estimate net salary and AVS/AI/IPG, AD, LAINF and LPP contributions, so as to have a clear picture of your contribution position before starting the procedure.

item.title: Rentals in Thurgau: average fees, deposit and conciliation
item.description: Rental market in the canton of Thurgau: how the security deposit works, when to challenge the initial rent and how to act before the conciliation authority.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Security deposit: maximum 3 months on a restricted account in the tenant's name - Cancellation of the landlord: valid only with the official cantonal form - Dispute of the initial fee: 30 days from the conciliation authority - Federal lease right: art. 253 et seq. CO, identical throughout Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: rental right applicable to rentals in the Canton of Thurgau - Where: Canton Thurgau, East German Switzerland - Who: tenants, landlords, cantonal conciliation authority - Legal basis: Code of Obligations (CO), art. 253 et seq. - Security deposit: maximum 3 months of rent, on a restricted account - Dispute deadline: 30 days from notification of the initial fee - Term of cancellation of the landlord: subject to official form of the Canton
The rental market in the canton of Thurgau is part of a uniform federal legal framework: Swiss rental law, governed by articles 253 et seq. of the Code of Obligations, applies identically in all cantons. This means that the minimum protections for the tenant — from the security deposit to the cancellation procedure up to the dispute terms — do not vary from Zurich to Bern or eastern Switzerland.
### The security deposit structure One of the most practical points concerns the security deposit. In Thurgau, as in the rest of Switzerland, the landlord can request a maximum of three months' gross rent. ### When to contest the initial rent One of the most important tools available to the tenant in Thurgau is the contestation of the initial rent. When the landlord announces a new rent — for example in the event of a change of tenant, adjustments following renovation work, or recalculations based on mortgage rates — the tenant may challenge it within 30 days before the rental conciliation authority of their district.
Contestation is not an unrestricted appeal: it must be based on grounds recognised under federal law, such as a rent deemed abusive compared to comparable rents in the area, or an adjustment not justified by an increase in costs or by objective improvements. The burden of substantiating the request often discourages weak challenges, but where the prerequisites are met, the procedure before the conciliation authority is free in its initial stages and may result in mediation or in a binding decision.
### Average rents: how to read market data The Canton of Thurgau has historically been characterised by lower average rents compared with economic hubs such as Zurich or Zug, but with steady growth driven by its proximity to St. Gallen and the Zurich conurbation. The data published by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS) on rental prices provide an overview by Canton and by region, broken down by housing category (number of rooms, year of construction). For a proper comparison, it is advisable to consult historical series rather than single data points: rents are surveyed on samples, and fluctuations of a few francs do not necessarily indicate a trend.
For those looking for housing in Thurgau, it is worth cross-referencing statistical data with concrete listings on property portals and bearing in mind that differences between rural municipalities and centres such as Frauenfeld or Kreuzlingen can be significant. Moreover, the market is influenced by the typical housing structure: in Thurgau, single-family homes and small condominium buildings predominate, whereas the supply of large rental properties is more limited.
### What happens if the landlord does not comply with the procedure If the landlord issues a termination without the official form, the tenant may challenge it and ask the conciliation authority to declare it invalid. The same applies if the security deposit exceeds three months' rent or if it has not been paid into a blocked account: established practice in Switzerland provides for the return of the excess and the regularisation of the position.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Operational procedure: how to proceed in practice When signing a rental contract in Thurgau, it is helpful to follow an essential checklist. Before signing, verify that the security deposit amount does not exceed three months of gross rent. Request written confirmation that the deposit will be placed in a blocked account held in the tenant's name or jointly held. Keep a copy of the contract, the housing condition report (Wohnungszustandsprotokoll) signed upon move-in, and all correspondence with the landlord.
If the landlord notifies a rent increase or a change in the initial rent, the tenant has 30 days to file an objection with the rental conciliation authority of their district. The procedure is accessible without legal assistance, but in the case of substantial amounts or complexity, it is advisable to contact a free legal advice centre available in the main centres of the Canton or the tenant associations active at regional level.
### Useful tools and contacts To understand the level of rents in your area, the reference source is the website of the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS), which regularly publishes data on the Swiss rental market. For the dispute procedure, the conciliation authority can be reached through the Canton of Thurgau's channels, and the official termination forms are available at municipal clerk's offices and online.
If you are considering a change of accommodation and want to simulate the impact of the new rent on your monthly budget, you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the net pay based on income and Canton. The real estate market must in fact be read together with actual purchasing power: a sustainable rent is one that does not erode the savings capacity needed for AVS, occupational pension (LPP) and the third pillar.
For those seeking broader guidance on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), including health insurance premiums and cantonal taxes, a complete overview is available on the site. The specific figures — LAMal premiums by region, LPP deductions, municipal multipliers — change every year and must be verified at the official source.

## In a nutshell - SNB reserves (excluding gold) increasing: from CHF 780 billion to CHF 782 billion - Total foreign currency assets increased to 771 billion, +1.9 billion in July - Euro at 0.9378 CHF (+0.9%), US dollar at 0.8089 CHF (+0.3%) - Dollar and euro cover about 80% of the SNB's foreign exchange reserves
## Key facts - **What**: Foreign currency reserves of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) increasing - When: Data reported at the end of August, published today - Where: Switzerland (institute based in Zurich and Bern) - Who: Swiss National Bank (SNB), led by Managing Director Martin Schlegel - Total amount of reserves (excluding gold): CHF 782 billion (from CHF 780 billion) - Amount of foreign currency assets: CHF 771 billion (+1.9 billion compared to July) - Euro/franc exchange rate: 0.9378 (end of August), compared to 0.9291 at the end of July - Dollar/franc exchange rate: 0.8089 (end of August), compared to 0.8064 at the end of July - Currency composition: US dollar and euro together represent about 80% of reserves
The foreign exchange reserves held by the Swiss National Bank increased again in August. According to data published on the institute's website, foreign currency assets amounted to CHF 771 billion, an increase of CHF 1.9 billion compared to the previous month.
### The detail of the monthly data Considering all reserves, excluding gold, the total rose from CHF 780 billion to CHF 782 billion. ## What the August variation really says
The August figure fits into a precise framework: the source indicates that fluctuations in reserves are not a rare event, but reflect two distinct phenomena. On the one hand, the evolution of currency markets, and on the other, possible monetary policy interventions. For the month under review, the SNB simply recorded the data, without announcing new measures.
The composition of the portfolio remains concentrated on two currencies: the dollar and the euro together account for about 80% of foreign exchange reserves. This share, quoted verbatim by the source, explains the sensitivity of the central bank's balance sheet to the monetary policy decisions of other central banks.
### How to read gearbox numbers
The strengthening of the euro against the franc (+0.9%) and the dollar (+0.3%) are limited movements but consistent with the overall increase in reserves expressed in francs. When the foreign currencies in which the reserves are invested appreciate compared to the franc, the value in francs rises even in the absence of new purchases.
Conversely, the source recalls that the institution has been making massive purchases of foreign currency for years, particularly after the abandonment of the minimum exchange rate threshold with the euro at the beginning of 2015. That change of course had led the franc to strengthen rapidly, with effects on the real Swiss economy that the SNB had countered by accumulating foreign currency assets.

Data on the SNB's foreign currency reserves are published on the bank's official website. The figures are released monthly and include both the total reserves (excluding gold) and the reference exchange rates for the main currencies.
### What the monthly statistics contain
The monthly statistics published by the SNB include the total amount of reserves (excluding gold), a breakdown of the main foreign currency items, and end-of-period exchange rates for the euro, the dollar, and other relevant currencies. For August, the source reports a move from 780 to 782 billion francs in total reserves (excluding gold) and from 769.1 to 771 billion in foreign currency assets, a change of +1.9 billion.
The euro/franc exchange rate at the end of August (0.9378) and dollar/franc (0.8089) can be directly compared with the end-of-July values previously published (0.9291 for the euro, 0.8064 for the dollar).
### Who needs to monitor these figures
Foreign currency reserves held by the central bank are an indicator followed by investors, financial analysts, economists, and foreign exchange market operators. Their change can offer clues — not confirmations — about the SNB's monetary policy stance, especially when currency purchases or sales deviate from simple portfolio revaluation.
For those who want to track trends over time, the SNB publishes historical series on its portal, where data on other balance sheet items are also available. The note released today contains no forecasts or qualitative indications on expected developments in the coming months: it simply reports the August figure and provides the exchange rate context.
